results.title: Minimax M3.1 Flash (Fully Tested): Okay, this MODEL is...
results.content:
Minimax M3.1 Flash preview is evaluated on the KingBench 3 coding benchmark across eight generation tasks (elevator sim, 3D contact lens case, folding table, panda SVG, archery game, math problem, local Gemma fine-tuning project, 3D watch). It scores 66.25% (53/80), a big jump from the earlier M3's 31.25%, but still trails top models like Opus 5.5 (93.75%), SWE2, and GPT6 Soul. Results are inconsistent: the folding table and contact lens case work well, while the elevator simulation and archery game have broken core interactions due to code bugs. Pricing and API details for this specific model remain unverified, with the public API still listing the older M3.

Questions this post answers [...] Not consistently. In testing, the elevator simulation crashed immediately because the code tried to call a position value as a function, scoring only 3 out of 10, and the archery game drew target graphics in the wrong location and had a timer that paused between shots, scoring 4 out of 10. Meanwhile the folding table task scored 9 out of 10 with smooth animated 3D geometry. developers weighing AI code-gen tools for real prototypes can follow hands-on test breakdowns like this via daily.dev.

results.title: MiniMax M3.1 Flash: 93% Hallucination Rate Found [2026]
results.content:
The broader market impact is that MiniMax has reinforced, rather than broken, the current equilibrium in the Flash-tier segment. No single model in this comparison dominates every axis: DeepSeek wins on raw intelligence-per-dollar, MiniMax wins on self-reported agent benchmarks in a few categories, Gemini trails on price but ties on capability, and Meta’s Muse Spark undercuts everyone on price for contributors willing to share usage data. That fragmentation is good news for buyers, who can increasingly shop by specific task type rather than committing to a single vendor, and it puts continued pressure on every lab in this tier to keep cutting prices or improving reliability metrics like the one Artificial Analysis just exposed in MiniMax’s model.

## Predictions: Where This Goes Next [...] SHATERED

# MiniMax M3.1 Flash Hits 93% Hallucination Rate 

Ryan Cole

Ryan Cole

Updated Oct 20, 2026 · 18 min read

MiniMax rolled out M3.1 Flash on October 19, 2026, pitching the model as a cheaper, faster option for agentic work, coding and computer-use tasks. Independent benchmarking from Artificial Analysis, reported by VentureBeat, backs up part of that pitch: the model’s Intelligence Index score jumped to 42 from 29 for its predecessor, while the average cost of completing a benchmark task dropped from roughly $0.51 to about $0.22. The same testing, though, surfaced a problem MiniMax did not mention in its own announcement: a 93% hallucination rate on a benchmark that measures how often a model gives a confidently wrong answer instead of admitting it does not know.

results.title: MiniMax M3.1 Flash Review: Specs, Pricing and Benchmarks
results.content:
Cons:

 Invented answers in 10 of 20 runs of questions about things that don't exist, and in 14 of 20 when told to say it didn't know
 Twice as slow per task as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash in our test, 16.5 seconds against 8.3
 Thinking can't be turned off, and at the default `max` effort it spent a median 49 seconds per coding task
 No published weights yet, and no local or self-hosted run

## Who should use MiniMax M3.1 Flash? [...] MiniMax M3.1 Flash, released on October 19, 2026, is a 1M-context reasoning model that always thinks; `reasoning_effort` from `low` to `max` sets how long.
 In our 51-run test on AI/ML API it passed 49, against 51 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and 50 each for GLM 5.3 Flash and MiniMax M3, and took twice as long per task as DeepSeek.
 It rarely admits not knowing: it invented answers in 10 of our 20 runs about nonexistent things, and Artificial Analysis measured a 92.8% hallucination rate, although it answered 56.2% of that test correctly, the most in its tier.
